Empirical Research Plan – “Investor Sentiment and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns”

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
Strategy chosen: Difference-in-Differences (panel DID with staggered “treatments” that turn on and off when aggregate sentiment is high).  

Why DID?  
• The key question is whether the return differential between sentiment-sensitive stocks (“speculative” firms) and sentiment-insensitive stocks (“stable” firms) widens when aggregate sentiment is high and narrows when sentiment is low.  
• We observe repeated switches between high- and low-sentiment months over a 50-year panel. The same firms are observed in both regimes, so we can difference out time-invariant firm heterogeneity and common macro shocks with two-way fixed effects.  
• DID is transparent, accommodates multiple switches, and lets us test pre-trends graphically and formally.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
Treatment variable  
Treated_i = 1 for firms that ex-ante theory predicts will be most affected by sentiment (small-cap, young, no-dividend, high volatility, low analyst coverage). Operationally, take the top quintile of a “speculativeness score” constructed each December t–1 and keep that classification fixed for year t. Score = size rank (ascending) + age rank (ascending) + payout rank (descending) + idiosyncratic‐volatility rank (descending).

Control group  
Firms in the bottom quintile of the same score (“stable” firms: large, mature, dividend-paying, low-volatility).

Treatment timing / event date  
HighSent_t = 1 in any month where the Baker–Wurgler composite sentiment index is above its 75th percentile over the estimation sample; HighSent_t = 0 when below its 25th percentile. Months in the inter-quartile range are dropped from the baseline regression to sharpen the contrast (keeps treatment clean; we re-introduce them in robustness checks).

The DID interaction is: Treated_i × HighSent_t.

(We do not need an RDD running variable or IV here, because assignment to HighSent_t is purely time-series and exogenous to individual firms.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
A. Parallel trends: In the absence of sentiment shocks, the average return gap between treated and control firms would have followed the same path.  
 Plausibility: These types of firms are exposed to aggregate risk differently, but two-way FE plus controls for macro factors (βs on Fama-French factors, macro surprises) largely absorb systematic differences. We will validate with event-study plots and placebo leads.

B. No simultaneous shocks differentially hitting treated vs. control in high-sentiment months.  
 Plausibility: Main macro news (recessions, rate cuts) is common; nonetheless, we will include month × sector fixed effects and macro controls.

C. Stable composition: Firms do not reclassify in response to sentiment within the year.  
 Plausibility: Classification is updated only once a year using lagged data, so reverse causality is limited.

D. SUTVA: Returns on one firm not affected by classification of another.  
 Plausibility: Reasonable given the broad market; sentiment spillovers should affect both groups similarly outside the treatment channel.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
1. Differential exposure to economic conditions  
   • Use month × Fama-French 10 industry FE and interact macro controls (GDP, CPI surprises) with Treated_i to absorb differential macro betas.  
   • Show results when matching treated and control firms on industry.

2. Sorting/selection into treated status  
   • Construct “speculativeness score” from lagged information only.  
   • Replicate analysis with continuous treatment (score × HighSent_t) and with propensity-score-weighted DID.

3. Measurement error in sentiment proxy  
   • Employ three alternative sentiment indices (U-Michigan surprise, VIX innovations sign-flipped, FEARS media index).  
   • Jackknife the BW index to confirm no single component drives results.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)     # Fast data handling
library(fixest)         # DID with high-dim FE
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------------------
ret  <- fread("monthly_stock_returns.csv")     # PERMNO, date, RET, MKTCAP, BM, AGE, DIV, ...
sent <- fread("sentiment_index.csv")           # date, BW_sent

# 2. Merge & variable construction ----------------------------------------
dt <- merge(ret, sent, by = "date")

# Build ‘speculativeness score’ using December t-1 firm data
dt[, year := year(date)]
base <- dt[month(date)==12]
base[, score :=
        frank(-MKTCAP, ties.method="average") +   # smaller = higher score
        frank(-AGE) +
        frank(-DIV) +
        frank(IDIO_VOL, ties.method="average") ]  # higher vol = higher score
base[, quintile := cut(score,
                       breaks = quantile(score, probs = seq(0,1,0.2), na.rm=TRUE),
                       labels = 1:5, include.lowest=TRUE)]

dt <- merge(dt, base[, .(PERMNO, year, quintile)], by = c("PERMNO","year"), all.x=TRUE)
dt[, treated := as.integer(quintile==5)]    # top quintile = treated
dt[, control := as.integer(quintile==1)]

# Sentiment dummy (75/25 rule)
q <- quantile(dt$BW_sent, probs = c(.25,.75), na.rm=TRUE)
dt[, highsent := BW_sent > q[2]]
dt[, lowsent  := BW_sent < q[1]]
dt <- dt[highsent==TRUE | lowsent==TRUE]    # Drop middle 50% for baseline

# 3. Main DID regression ---------------------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(RET ~ treated*highsent +
                  MKT_RF + SMB + HML + MOM | PERMNO + date, data = dt,
                  cluster = ~date)           # Cluster on month
summary(did_main)

# 4. Event-study / pre-trend check ----------------------------------------
es <- feols(RET ~ i(k, treated, ref=-1) |
            PERMNO + date,
            data = dt[, k := -6:6 + .GRP, by=.(highsent, date)], cluster=~date)

iplot(es)   # Visual check

# 5. Robustness: Alternative sentiment index ------------------------------
alt <- fread("umich_surprise.csv")        # macro surprise series
dt2 <- merge(ret, alt, by="date")
# ... replicate above, swap in alt_sent ...

# 6. Save results
saveRDS(did_main, "results/did_main.rds")
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
Theory (e.g., Baker & Wurgler, 2006) predicts that when sentiment is high, speculative, hard-to-value stocks become over-priced, generating lower subsequent returns relative to stable firms.  
Therefore β3 (treated × highsent) should be negative: speculative stocks underperform stable stocks by, say, 40–60 bps per month (≈5–7 % annualized) after high-sentiment months. In low-sentiment months, the gap should shrink or even reverse.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)

C1: Parallel pre-trends clearly demonstrated in event-study graph ………………… 1  
C2: No differential concurrent shocks (addressed with controls) ………………… 0.8  
C3: No anticipatory trading around sentiment switches ……………………………… 0.8  
C4: Stable classification and no sorting on future sentiment …………………… 0.9  
C5: SUTVA (no spillovers) ………………………………………………………………… 0.9  
Average ≈ 0.88 → Overall credible but not bullet-proof; robustness exercises are essential.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
